# Unbiased mosaic variant assessment in sperm: a cohort study to test predictability of transmission

## Authors

- Martin W Breuss<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0003-2200-8604](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2200-8604)) †
- Xiaoxu Yang<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0003-0219-0023](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0219-0023))
- Valentina Stanley<sup>1</sup>
- Jennifer McEvoy-Venneri<sup>1</sup>
- Xin Xu<sup>1</sup>
- Arlene J Morales<sup>4</sup>
- Joseph G Gleeson<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-0889-9220](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0889-9220)) †

### Affiliations

1. Rady Children’s Institute for Genomic Medicine San Diego United States
2. Department of Neurosciences, University of California, San Diego La Jolla United States ([ROR:0168r3w48](https://ror.org/0168r3w48))
3. Department of Pediatrics, Section of Clinical Genetics and Metabolism, University of Colorado School of Medicine Aurora United States
4. Fertility Specialists Medical Group San Diego United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Background:De novo mutations underlie individually rare but collectively common pediatric congenital disorders. Some of these mutations can also be detected in tissues and from cells in a parent, where their abundance and tissue distribution can be measured. We previously reported that a subset of these mutations is detectable in sperm from the father, predicted to impact the health of offspring.Methods:As a cohort study, in three independent couples undergoing in vitro fertilization, we first identified male gonadal mosaicism through deep whole genome sequencing. We then confirmed variants and assessed their transmission to preimplantation blastocysts (32 total) through targeted ultra-deep genotyping.Results:Across 55 gonadal mosaic variants, 15 were transmitted to blastocysts for a total of 19 transmission events. This represented an overall predictable but slight undertransmission based upon the measured mutational abundance in sperm. We replicated this conclusion in an independent, previously published family-based cohort.Conclusions:Unbiased preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism may represent a feasible approach to reduce the transmission of potentially harmful de novo mutations. This—in turn—could help to reduce their impact on miscarriages and pediatric disease.Funding:No external funding was received for this work.

## Introduction

Genomic mosaic mutations—present in some but not all cells within a tissue—record the history of embryonic development, environmental exposure, and have a wide range of implications for human health (Biesecker and Spinner, 2013; Paquola et al., 2017). Mosaic mutations are commonly recognized in cancers or localized overgrowth disorders, such as Proteus, CLOVES, and hemimegalencephaly syndromes (Lee et al., 2012; Lindhurst et al., 2011; Goncalves et al., 2018). Increasingly recognized in more complex diseases such as autism spectrum disorder or structural abnormalities (Jamuar et al., 2014; Rodin et al., 2021,) mosaic mutations are typically restricted to the individual in which they arise unless they appear prior to the embryonic separation of somatic and germline lineages or within germ cell progenitors. In these cases, gonadal mosaic mutations (comprising gonad specific and gonosomal) have the potential to transmit to offspring. These will appear as a considerable portion of de novo mutations and may result in miscarriage or a congenital or complex disease—often without phenotypes in the parents (Breuss et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2020).

We and others previously demonstrated that 5–20% of identified pathogenic de novo mutations in a child are detectable in parental tissues, with ejaculated sperm demonstrating the highest rate of occurrence (Yang et al., 2020; Breuss et al., 2020; Myers et al., 2018). Every male harbors up to dozens of such mutations in sperm, which—in contrast to other paternal mutation types that increase with age (Jónsson et al., 2017)—contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age (Yang et al., 2021). As such, they are thought to explain, in part, the individually rare but collectively common risk of congenital disorders from de novo mutations (Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2017). Yet, experimental evidence of transmission to a conceptus of in situ identified gonadal mosaic mutations—in contrast to the detection of gonadal mosaicism of already transmitted variants—is lacking. This is a critical point upon which clinical implementation hinges because procedures like preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) could be used to select embryos absent for potentially damaging mutations detected in sperm. Here, we demonstrate that gonadal mosaic mutations detected in sperm from individual males can transmit to their preimplantation blastocysts. We decided to assess this early time point, as it avoids any potential bias introduced by a possible selection of mosaic mutations or their lineages during implantation or survival.

## Methods

### Donor population, recruitment, and sample preparation

For gonadal mosaicism assessment, we recruited three infertile couples (F01, F02, and F03) who had supernumerary blastocysts (minimum of 8) that wanted to donate them to research. The males (‘sperm donors’) all provided a fresh ejaculate and a somatic sample (blood for F01, saliva for F02 and F03). The age of the three sperm donors was 36, 38, and 50 years for F01, F02, and F03, respectively. In accordance with reported population origin, the three fathers’ ancestries were most closely matched to Middle Eastern (F01) or European (F02 and F03) ancestry, employing nearest neighbor analysis of principle components (Taliun et al., 2017). One of the three females (‘egg donors’) was a nonidentified egg donor (F01) and provided blood, another woman was the partner (F02) and provided saliva. The third chose not to provide a somatic sample (F03). DNA was extracted from each parental sample using documented procedures (Breuss et al., 2020), and extracted and amplified from vitrified blastocysts by thawing in phosphate-buffered saline supplemented with 5% bovine serum albumin and processing with REPLI-g whole-genome amplification methods (Qiagen, Cat. #150343). Informed consent was obtained from all participants (custodians of the blastocysts) as well as from each participant in a study protocol approved by the University of California, San Diego IRB (140028).

### Whole-genome sequencing and massive parallel sequencing

Whole-genome sequencing (WGS; NovaSeq 6000, Illumina) of the sperm donor samples was performed to approximately 300× (Supplementary file 1) as described (Yang et al., 2021), then analyzed using the 300× MSMF (MuTect2, Strelka2, MosaicForecast) computational pipeline (Yang et al., 2021). This pipeline demonstrates a 90% specificity and sensitivity of >95% for mutations at allelic fractions (AFs) above 0.03 (Ref Yang et al., 2021). All putative mosaic mutations (single-nucleotide variants and small insertion–deletion mutations only) as well as 120 common and rare single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), each detected as heterozygous in only one of the sperm donors, were then subjected to validation using massive parallel amplicon sequencing (MPAS, AmpliSeq Illumina Custom DNA Panel), to orthogonally assess each mutation in sperm donors, egg donors, and blastocysts. We also included two unrelated controls to control for false-positive calls (Supplementary file 1; Breuss et al., 2022).

### MPAS data analysis

Mosaic mutations from tissues or blastocysts were confirmed or rejected based on the distribution of reference homozygous mutations and the signal in control samples at the same position as described previously (Breuss et al., 2022). The overall number and distribution of mosaic mutations were largely consistent with other unbiased analyses performed previously (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). SNPs in nonblastocyst samples were assigned genotypes as reference homozygous, heterozygous, or alternate homozygous, based on the appearance of known genotypes previously determined in WGS data. Blastocysts were determined as genotype negative or positive for the SNPs.

To determine the expected number of transmissions to each blastocyst, the list of gonadal mosaic mutations and their measured AF in sperm for each sperm donor was used to determine the expected probability of transmission. Then, each blastocyst was combined with all other blastocysts from a single sperm donor or across all sperm donors as indicated. A Gaussian 1D model was fitted using astropy’s LevMarLSQFitter and Gaussian1D to obtain the mean as well as the standard deviation and 95% confidence interval. Code used for data analysis and generation of all plots can be found on GitHub: https://github.com/shishenyxx/Sperm_transmission_mosaicism; Yang, 2022. Blastocysts with less than 10% detectable genomic positions according to the panel were excluded from the downstream analysis.

### Determination of false-negative and -positive rate of transmission to blastocysts

To calibrate our genotyping approach on whole-genome-amplified blastocyst material, we determined the transmission of heterozygous variants from sperm and egg donors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). We found that transmission followed expected genetic patterns; furthermore, homozygous variants from a parent—which should be present across all blastocysts—were transmitted in approximately 94% of those analyzed, suggesting a false-negative rate of ~0.06. Importantly, this false-negative rate also includes potential allelic dropout, which can be problematic for single-cell studies or amplification from biopsies. Conversely, when assessing the presence of gonadal mosaic mutations identified in one sperm donor in the blastocysts of the other two, we only found one such event out of 985 possible, suggesting an MPAS false-positive rate of ~0.001. Thus, this approach provides sensitivity to detect clinically relevant gonadal mosaicism (i.e., mutations with a measurable and potentially actionably abundance) and specificity to assess transmissions of perm mosaic mutations to blastocysts, and it suggests that whole-genome-amplified blastocysts exhibit modest allelic dropout, even though allelic imbalance was frequently observed.

### Determination of mosaicism in MPAS data

For each mosaic mutation or SNP, we determined the estimated AF and its 95% confidence interval based on MPAS. As a baseline for observed noise, we determined the distribution of reference homozygous SNPs and their lower 95% confidence interval (population threshold). Mutations considered as a mosaic in a sperm donor’s tissue fulfilled three criteria: (1) read depth for the position was at least 100×; (2) the observed 95% confidence interval of the mutation did not overlap with the population threshold or the upper 95% confidence interval of the control samples; (3) either control’s lower 95% confidence interval limit had to be below the population threshold. For a blastocyst, to be considered positive for the mutation, similar criteria were applied, but the lower 95% confidence interval could not overlap with 0.05 AF and the read depth at this position had to be equal or above 20×. For SNPs in blood, saliva, and sperm, a mutation was considered heterozygous if above or equal to 0.2 and below 0.8 AF; it was considered homozygous if above or equal to 0.8 AF. Blastocysts were considered positive (either heterozygous or homozygous, not distinguished) if above 0.05 AF.

### Determination of evenness of ransmitted mutations across blastocysts

For each of F01, F02, and F03, the observed number of transmitted mutations was randomly assigned to the different blastocysts in 10,000 permutations. For each permutation, the maximum number of mutations transmitted to one blastocyst as well as the standard deviation of the number of mutations transmitted across each blastocyst was determined. The obtained distribution across the 10,000 permutations was then compared to the observed value. A permutation p value was calculated based on the tail probability (the number of permuted values larger than or equal to the observed value over the total number of permutations).

### Distribution and impact of gonadal mosaic mutations

The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across all chromosomes—except for chromosomes 19, 22, and X/Y—roughly as expected based on chromosomal length. As expected based on prior work, the vast majority was found in intergenic (n = 28) or intronic (n = 24) regions; one mutation each was found in a 5′-UTR, the intron of a noncoding RNA, and an exon. The exonic mutation (F03, AF = 0.063) resulted in a nonsynonymous SNV in RABGAP1 (NM_012197; p.Asp74Gly), a rare, previously reported mutation (allele frequency of 7.96e−6) with no known disease association.

### Reanalysis of the REACH cohort

Reanalysis of the REACH cohort data was performed by combining the list of detected gonadal mosaic mutation (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021) with previously established variants called from the trio WGS (Brandler et al., 2018; Brandler et al., 2016). For each gonadal mosaic mutation, we determined the occurrence in a child similar to what was done for blastocysts. Finally, the expected probability of transmission was determined as described above.

## Results

We recruited three couples undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) for infertility (F01, F02, and F03), where at least eight blastocysts each were donated for research (Supplementary file 1). DNA was extracted from each sample, including paternal sperm, using standard procedures (Breuss et al., 2020), and blastocysts underwent whole-genome amplification. Tissue-specific and -shared mosaicism was determined for each donor (F01–F03) in sperm and one somatic tissue (i.e., blood or saliva) as described (Yang et al., 2021; Figure 1a). WGS of sperm samples to 300× read depth allowed ‘best practice’ detection of mosaicism (Yang et al., 2021). The computational pipeline demonstrates 90% specificity and >95% sensitivity for mosaic mutation detection at AFs above 0.03 (Yang et al., 2021). All putative mosaic mutations and additional control SNPs from the sperm donors were then subjected to validation using MPAS, AmpliSeq for Illumina Custom DNA Panel (Breuss et al., 2022). This was done for both tissues of the sperm donor, one somatic tissue of the egg donor if provided (F01 and F02), and all available blastocysts.

![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 1.:** (a) Overview of the employed workflow from mutation detection to validation and prediction. A single massive parallel amplicon sequencing (MPAS) panel was used for both detections of mutations in parental tissues and in preimplantation blastocysts. WGS: whole-genome sequencing; 300× MSMF: variant calling pipeline on 300× WGS data using MuTect2, Strelka2, and MosaicForecast (Yang et al., 2021). (b) The number of MPAS-validated gonadal mosaic mutations for each sperm donor, distinguished by color into sperm-specific (‘Sperm’, green) and tissue-shared (‘Shared’, brown) mutations. (c) Ranked plot of all gonadal mosaic mutations across the three sperm donors. For each variant, both the allelic fraction (AF; normalized to chromosome count) of the mutation in sperm (green line) and in the soma (brown dot) are shown together with their 95% exact confidence interval. Shared mutations tend to be of higher AF compared to Sperm.

![Figure 1—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig1-figsupp1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 1—figure supplement 1.:** (a) Total number of identified mosaic single-nucleotide mutations (mSNVs) and mosaic small insertions and deletions (mINDELs) across the three sperm donors. Mosaic mutations are divided into those detected only in sperm (‘Sperm’), those detected in both sperm and the somatic tissue (‘Shared’), and those detected only in the somatic tissue (‘Soma’; i.e., blood or saliva). (b) The number of mosaic mutations for each individual for each category. (c) Ranked plots for mosaic mutations across all sperm donors for each category. Shown are the allelic fractions (AFs; normalized to chromosome counts) within the indicated tissue(s) and their 95% exact confidence interval. (d) Distribution of square root-transformed (sqrt-t) AFs for each sperm donor for each category as a violin plot.

The three sperm donors harbored a combined 55 detected gonadal mosaic mutations—mostly single-nucleotide mutations—with the potential to be transmitted to offspring (F01: 12, F02: 13, and F03: 30) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1). While F01 and F02 differed by more than twofold from F03, this likely represents expected biological variability that is within the previously observed range (Yang et al., 2021). None of the variants were predicted to impair health when heterozygous, and they, thus, serve as likely neutral variants to model transmission. These mutations were present at AFs between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055), with those of lower AF typically restricted to sperm (‘Sperm’) and those of higher AF typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva (‘Shared’) (Figure 1c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1). Overall, their number, distribution, and abundance were consistent with other unbiased analyses performed previously (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). Of note, similar to our prior observations (Yang et al., 2021), the sperm donor F01 (36 years of age) had an excessive number of soma-specific mutations (‘Soma’) at lower AFs, evidencing early clonal hematopoiesis (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

For each sperm donor, 8, 10, or 14 blastocysts, respectively (total: N = 32), were assessed for transmission of paternal gonadal mosaic mutations. When calibrating our genotyping approach on whole-genome-amplified blastocyst material, we found a false-negative rate of ~0.06 and a false-positive rate of ~0.001 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Across all 55 identified gonadal mosaic mutations, we observed 19 transmission events among 15 unique mutations (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1). For F02, two of the eight blastocysts did not show overall high quality in the MPAS for gonadal mosaic variants and thus were excluded from subsequent analyses.

![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig2-v1.jpg)

**Figure 2.:** Mutations are ranked for each sperm donor by allelic fraction (AF) and visualized as square root-transformed (sqrt-t). Shown are the transmission of 12 mutations across 10 blastocysts (F01), of 13 mutations across 6 blastocysts (F02; 2 of 8 blastocysts did not show sufficient read depth across the mosaic mutations), and of 30 mutations across 14 blastocysts. In total, 19 transmissions of 15 unique mutations were observed. As expected, gonadal mosaic mutations of higher AF are more likely to transmit than those of lower AF. No Data: variant blastocyst pairs, for which read depth was below 20×.

![Figure 2—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig2-figsupp1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 2—figure supplement 1.:** (a) Transmission of heterozygous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) detected in at least one parental genome. Parental genotypes are indicated as reference homozygous (0/0) and heterozygous (0/1). The 95% confidence interval of the observed fraction of transmissions overlaps with expectations of 0.5 (parents are heterozygous and reference homozygous, respectively) and 0.75 (parents are both heterozygous). 0/0 and 0/1: n = 374 transmitted of 736 total; 0/1 and 0/1: n = 129 transmitted of 170 total. As egg donor information was missing in F03, this analysis is restricted to F01 and F02. (b) Fraction of blastocysts that were determined to be negative when one of the parental genotypes is homozygous for an SNP (1/1). As a homozygous parent is expected to transmit the SNP to each blastocyst this allows us to determine the false-negative rate (FNR = 0.058). 0/0 and 1/1: n = 81 transmitted of 86 total. As egg donor information was missing in F03, this analysis is restricted to F01 and F02. (c) Fraction of blastocysts that were determined to be positive when the mosaic mutation was identified in one of the unrelated sperm donors. These transmissions are unexpected and can only be explained by a technical artifact, allowing us to determine the false-positive rate (FPR = 0.001). Nonmosaic: n = 1 ‘transmitted’ of 985 total.

![Figure 2—figure supplement 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig2-figsupp2-v1.jpg)

**Figure 2—figure supplement 2.:** Permutation analysis for the observed number of transmitted mutations across blastocyst for F01 (a), F02 (b), and F03 (c), respectively. Underlying data points are either the maximum observed number of mutations within one blastocyst (top, Max. Number of Mutations/Blastocyst) or the standard deviation of the observed number of mutations across all blastocysts (bottom, Standard Deviation of Mutations/Blastocyst) (n = 10,000 permutations). Graphs show the density distribution of all permutations (green dashed line) and the corresponding observed value (vertical red line). Note that in F03, both the observed maximum number of transmitted mutations within one blastocyst and the standard deviation of observed transmissions across all blastocysts were significantly different from the random permutations (p < 0.05).

Consistent with a model where the risk of transmission is proportional to sperm AF, mutations of higher AF evidenced higher blastocyst transmission rates than those of lower AF (R = 0.67, p value = 2.9e−8, Pearson correlation, Methods). Although additional mutations may arise within earlier sperm lineages marked by prior mutations (e.g., blastocyst #2 in F03), somewhat unexpectedly, we observed cosegregation of mutations of almost equal AF (e.g., blastocyst #1 in F02 or blastocyst #6 in F03); this was reflected as a nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts in F03 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). This suggests that some early male germ cell lineages or individual mitotic divisions are more susceptible to mutation than others, allowing stratification of sperm lineages into those with higher and those with lower mosaic load, and mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis. Indeed, we observed different combinations of gonadal mosaic mutations across blastocysts (e.g., blastocysts #5, #6, and #9 in F03). This analysis demonstrates that a priori identified gonadal mosaic mutations have the potential to transmit to preimplantation blastocysts.

Based upon their individually measured AFs, we next calculated the expected number of transmission events across all blastocysts. Whereas for both F01 and F02 the observed transmission rate was within the 95% confidence interval of the expectation, for F03 and across all individuals when considered in total, the transmission was slightly below what was expected (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This likely reflects a limitation of the model which assumes that gonadal mosaic mutations arise and transmit independently—a simplification, as mutations arising on the same lineage have the potential to cotransmit. This may be especially relevant if sperm lineages do not stochastically accumulate mutations during early development. Nevertheless, our observations closely reflect expectations, suggesting that gonadal mosaicism assessment can serve as a predictor of mutation transmission.

![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig3-v1.jpg)

**Figure 3.:** The expected number of transmissions—based on the allelic fraction (AF) of all detected mutations in sperm and the number of analyzed blastocysts—is indicated with the mean and a 95% confidence interval for each sperm donor and across all sperm donors. Whereas F01 and F02 transmitted as expected, F03 showed a slight undertransmission, likely related to the nonindependence of mutations due to shared lineage.

![Figure 3—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig3-figsupp1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 3—figure supplement 1.:** (a–d) Probability of the number of expected transmission events (gray bars), a Gaussian fit (green dashed line tracing the bars), the 95% confidence intervals if not 0 (vertical green dashed lines), and the observed number of transmission (vertical red line). This is shown for each sperm donor and blastocysts group (F01, F02, and F03 in a, b, and c, respectively) and across all (d). The mean and standard deviation determined from the Gaussian fit were used to generate data shown in Figure 3.

![Figure 3—figure supplement 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78459/elife-78459-fig3-figsupp2-v1.jpg)

**Figure 3—figure supplement 2.:** (a) Transmission of gonadal mosaic mutations for each of eight fathers whose gonadal mosaicism was previously described (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). Each family had one to three offspring for whom variants were called from standard whole-genome sequencing (Brandler et al., 2016). Mutations are ranked for each father by allelic fraction (AF) and visualized as square root-transformed (sqrt-t). Shown are the transmission of 19 mutations to 1 child (REACH-F01), of 11 mutations to 1 child (REACH-F02), 14 mutations across 2 children (REACH-F03), 18 mutations across 2 children (REACH-F04), 11 mutations across 2 children (REACH-F05), 19 mutations across 2 children (REACH-F06), 14 mutations to 1 child (REACH-F07), and of 25 mutations across 3 children (REACH-F08). In total, 9 transmissions of 7 unique mutations were observed. (b) Expected number of transmissions—based on the AF of all detected mutations in sperm and the number of analyzed children—is indicated with the mean and a 95% confidence interval for each father and across all fathers. Whereas, individually, each father transmitted within expectations, collectively, all fathers exhibited a slight undertransmission, comparable to what was found for blastocysts and F01–F03. (c) Probability of the number of expected transmission events across all fathers, visualized as in Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The mean and standard deviation determined from the Gaussian fit were used to generate data shown in b.

To validate the observation of predictable transmission and slight undertransmission, we further analyzed our previous gonadal mosaicism data from 8 families with a total of 14 offspring, where we reported between 11 and 25 sperm-detectable mosaic variants per father (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). We asked whether variants detected in sperm employing our unbiased detection pipeline transmitted to any of the 14 offspring. Across 131 sperm-detectable mosaic variants, we observed nine transmissions among seven unique variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and Supplementary file 1). As this cohort had a lower number of observable transmission events per paternal sample due to the lower number of fertilization events (1–3 offspring compared to 8–14 blastocysts) and lower sequencing depth, we combined analysis of the eight families. The observed transmission rate was again slightly below the expected 95% confidence interval (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, c). This replication in live-born offspring supports the undertransmission observed in blastocysts and highlights the potential predictive power of gonadal mosaicism assessment.

## Discussion

Here, we directly measured the abundance of gonadal mosaic variants and demonstrate transmission to preimplantation blastocysts for three couples undergoing IVF. These results provide a proof-of-concept that a priori detected gonadal mosaic mutations can transmit to blastocysts and therefore likely to offspring. There are two important limitations of our study: (1) we were only able to ascertain this phenomenon in three sperm donors and their associated blastocysts; (2) none of the variants interrogated for this study were predicted to be disease causing. Thus, if this approach is to be advanced in the clinic to prevent genetic disease, further research is necessary that expands the size of the cohort and directly assesses a priori identified pathogenic variants for transmission to blastocysts. In addition, further technological development will be required to enable the direct assessment of mutations from biopsies rather than whole blastocysts as implemented in this study.

Previous studies focused on the detection of mosaicism in parents following the identification of de novo mutations in offspring (Breuss et al., 2020; Rahbari et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2018). Currently, following the birth of a child with a disease due to a de novo mutation, parents are provided with an empirical recurrence risk of 1–2% for future pregnancies. However, this population risk reflects an average of a near-zero risk in the majority and measurably higher risk (up to 25%) in a minority of instances due to gonadal mosaicism (Campbell et al., 2014). While recent studies have improved the risk accuracy by incorporating population models and sampling parental blood (Jónsson et al., 2018; Campbell et al., 2014), direct assessment of gonadal mosaicism can provide a more precise personalized risk, as well as the potential to prevent recurrence through genetic testing. Yet, this framework is only applicable to families where a de novo mutations has previously been identified, and it can merely prevent recurrence within a family. While we previously demonstrated our ability to detect gonadal mosaicism in males independent of prior transmission (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021), this study provides the important complement that these detected variants are, indeed, transmitted to the next generation.

What is the potential health impact of the detection of gonadal mosaic variants and their prevention before any child is born with disease? We previously estimated that 1 in 15 males carry a potentially pathogenic mutation, detectable in approximately 5% of sperm cells (Yang et al., 2021). Together, this led to a prediction that a gonadal mosaic variant may result in adverse pregnancy or pediatric health outcomes for 1 in 300 concepti (Yang et al., 2021). While this likely only represents ~15% of the monogenic sporadic component of diseases such as autism or congenital heart disease, this is the sole fraction that could be prevented with further advances. Thus, if these mosaic mutations were detected prior to pregnancy, and if mutation-carrying blastocysts were identified by PGT, there could be positive consequences for families through the prevention of pregnancy termination or pediatric diseases.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.78459.sa0](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.78459.sa0)

This manuscript confirms and extends a recent study from this same group analyzing mosaicism in sperm and transmission of new mutations to relevant offspring. The current work extends previous analysis of mosaicism in sperm to human blastocysts from in vitro fertilization for three subjects (a total of 55 blastocysts), demonstrating transmission of mosaic mutations at close to expected frequencies. The experiments and analysis are carefully done and of high quality, with potential translational relevance to the diagnosis and prevention of genetic disease by pre-implantation genetic testing for a limited subset of mutations.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.78459.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.78459.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Sperm mosaicism predicts transmission of de novo mutations to human blastocysts" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, including David Ginsburg as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Ricardo Azziz as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential Revisions:

1) In Figure 1b – Individual F03 has more than twice as many mosaic variants as F01 or F02. Is there a difference in sequence depth, age, or another explanation? Is the difference statistically significant?

Additional comments/suggestions for authors:

1) The manuscript is well-written and the figures are generally clear. However, this is a specialized field and some of the genetic concepts are quite complex and may be of limited accessibility to the general reader. The authors might consider trying to provide a more general and accessible summary of the work and findings and their implications, including the limitation to only a relatively small subset of de novo genetic mutations.

claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach and sample size used in the study.

claims.claim: Across 55 gonadal mosaic variants, 15 were transmitted to blastocysts for a total of 19 transmission events.
claims.source: Across 55 gonadal mosaic variants, 15 were transmitted to blastocysts for a total of 19 transmission events.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results from the study.

claims.claim: The transmission represented an overall predictable but slight undertransmission based upon the measured mutational abundance in sperm.
claims.source: This represented an overall predictable but slight undertransmission based upon the measured mutational abundance in sperm.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data comparing observed to expected transmission rates.

claims.claim: The conclusion of predictable transmission and slight undertransmission was replicated in an independent, previously published family-based cohort.
claims.source: We replicated this conclusion in an independent, previously published family-based cohort.
claims.evidence: This describes replication analysis using previously published data.

claims.claim: Unbiased preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism may represent a feasible approach to reduce the transmission of potentially harmful de novo mutations.
claims.source: Unbiased preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism may represent a feasible approach to reduce the transmission of potentially harmful de novo mutations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings about the potential clinical application.

claims.claim: Preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism could help to reduce the impact of de novo mutations on miscarriages and pediatric disease.
claims.source: This—in turn—could help to reduce their impact on miscarriages and pediatric disease.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical benefits based on the study findings.

claims.claim: Mosaic mutations are commonly recognized in cancers or localized overgrowth disorders, such as Proteus, CLOVES, and hemimegalencephaly syndromes.
claims.source: Mosaic mutations are commonly recognized in cancers or localized overgrowth disorders, such as Proteus, CLOVES, and hemimegalencephaly syndromes (Lee et al., 2012; Lindhurst et al., 2011; Goncalves et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on mosaic mutations in various disorders.

claims.claim: Mosaic mutations are increasingly recognized in more complex diseases such as autism spectrum disorder or structural abnormalities.
claims.source: Increasingly recognized in more complex diseases such as autism spectrum disorder or structural abnormalities (Jamuar et al., 2014; Rodin et al., 2021,) mosaic mutations are typically restricted to the individual in which they arise unless they appear prior to the embryonic separation of somatic and germline lineages or within germ cell progenitors.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to research on mosaic mutations in complex diseases.

claims.claim: Mosaic mutations are typically restricted to the individual in which they arise unless they appear prior to the embryonic separation of somatic and germline lineages or within germ cell progenitors.
claims.source: Increasingly recognized in more complex diseases such as autism spectrum disorder or structural abnormalities (Jamuar et al., 2014; Rodin et al., 2021,) mosaic mutations are typically restricted to the individual in which they arise unless they appear prior to the embryonic separation of somatic and germline lineages or within germ cell progenitors.
claims.evidence: This describes the biological basis for when mosaic mutations can be transmitted, based on established developmental biology knowledge.

claims.claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations have the potential to transmit to offspring.
claims.source: In these cases, gonadal mosaic mutations (comprising gonad specific and gonosomal) have the potential to transmit to offspring.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the timing of mutation occurrence relative to germline development.

claims.claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations may result in miscarriage or a congenital or complex disease—often without phenotypes in the parents.
claims.source: These will appear as a considerable portion of de novo mutations and may result in miscarriage or a congenital or complex disease—often without phenotypes in the parents (Breuss et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on the consequences of gonadal mosaic mutations.

claims.claim: 5–20% of identified pathogenic de novo mutations in a child are detectable in parental tissues.
claims.source: We and others previously demonstrated that 5–20% of identified pathogenic de novo mutations in a child are detectable in parental tissues, with ejaculated sperm demonstrating the highest rate of occurrence (Yang et al., 2020; Breuss et al., 2020; Myers et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple prior studies quantifying parental mosaicism.

claims.claim: Ejaculated sperm demonstrates the highest rate of occurrence of detectable pathogenic de novo mutations among parental tissues.
claims.source: We and others previously demonstrated that 5–20% of identified pathogenic de novo mutations in a child are detectable in parental tissues, with ejaculated sperm demonstrating the highest rate of occurrence (Yang et al., 2020; Breuss et al., 2020; Myers et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research comparing mutation detection rates across tissues.

claims.claim: Every male harbors up to dozens of gonadal mosaic mutations in sperm.
claims.source: Every male harbors up to dozens of such mutations in sperm, which—in contrast to other paternal mutation types that increase with age (Jónsson et al., 2017)—contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age (Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research quantifying gonadal mosaic mutations in males.

claims.claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age.
claims.source: Every male harbors up to dozens of such mutations in sperm, which—in contrast to other paternal mutation types that increase with age (Jónsson et al., 2017)—contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age (Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research on the age-independence of gonadal mosaic mutations.

claims.claim: Other paternal mutation types increase with age.
claims.source: Every male harbors up to dozens of such mutations in sperm, which—in contrast to other paternal mutation types that increase with age (Jónsson et al., 2017)—contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age (Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research on age-related paternal mutations.

claims.claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations are thought to explain, in part, the individually rare but collectively common risk of congenital disorders from de novo mutations.
claims.source: As such, they are thought to explain, in part, the individually rare but collectively common risk of congenital disorders from de novo mutations (Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research on the contribution of de novo mutations to congenital disorders.

claims.claim: Experimental evidence of transmission to a conceptus of in situ identified gonadal mosaic mutations is lacking.
claims.source: Yet, experimental evidence of transmission to a conceptus of in situ identified gonadal mosaic mutations—in contrast to the detection of gonadal mosaicism of already transmitted variants—is lacking.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: Procedures like preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) could be used to select embryos absent for potentially damaging mutations detected in sperm.
claims.source: This is a critical point upon which clinical implementation hinges because procedures like preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) could be used to select embryos absent for potentially damaging mutations detected in sperm.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications based on the study's premise.

claims.claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations detected in sperm from individual males can transmit to their preimplantation blastocysts.
claims.source: Here, we demonstrate that gonadal mosaic mutations detected in sperm from individual males can transmit to their preimplantation blastocysts.
claims.evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The study assessed transmission at the preimplantation blastocyst stage to avoid potential bias introduced by selection of mosaic mutations or their lineages during implantation or survival.
claims.source: We decided to assess this early time point, as it avoids any potential bias introduced by a possible selection of mosaic mutations or their lineages during implantation or survival.
claims.evidence: This explains the rationale for the study design choice based on methodological considerations.

claims.claim: Three infertile couples (F01, F02, and F03) who had supernumerary blastocysts (minimum of 8) were recruited for gonadal mosaicism assessment.
claims.source: For gonadal mosaicism assessment, we recruited three infertile couples (F01, F02, and F03) who had supernumerary blastocysts (minimum of 8) that wanted to donate them to research.
claims.evidence: This describes the study population and recruitment criteria.

claims.claim: The males provided a fresh ejaculate and a somatic sample (blood for F01, saliva for F02 and F03).
claims.source: The males ('sperm donors') all provided a fresh ejaculate and a somatic sample (blood for F01, saliva for F02 and F03).
claims.evidence: This describes the sample collection from study participants.

claims.claim: The age of the three sperm donors was 36, 38, and 50 years for F01, F02, and F03, respectively.
claims.source: The age of the three sperm donors was 36, 38, and 50 years for F01, F02, and F03, respectively.
claims.evidence: This provides demographic information about the study participants.

claims.claim: The three fathers' ancestries were most closely matched to Middle Eastern (F01) or European (F02 and F03) ancestry.
claims.source: In accordance with reported population origin, the three fathers' ancestries were most closely matched to Middle Eastern (F01) or European (F02 and F03) ancestry, employing nearest neighbor analysis of principle components (Taliun et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the genetic ancestry analysis of the study participants.

claims.claim: Whole-genome sequencing of the sperm donor samples was performed to approximately 300× read depth.
claims.source: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS; NovaSeq 6000, Illumina) of the sperm donor samples was performed to approximately 300× (Supplementary file 1) as described (Yang et al., 2021), then analyzed using the 300× MSMF (MuTect2, Strelka2, MosaicForecast) computational pipeline (Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: The 300× MSMF computational pipeline demonstrates a 90% specificity and sensitivity of >95% for mutations at allelic fractions above 0.03.
claims.source: This pipeline demonstrates a 90% specificity and sensitivity of >95% for mutations at allelic fractions (AFs) above 0.03 (Ref Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This describes the performance characteristics of the computational pipeline, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The false-negative rate for transmission detection in whole-genome-amplified blastocyst material is approximately 0.06.
claims.source: We found that transmission followed expected genetic patterns; furthermore, homozygous variants from a parent—which should be present across all blastocysts—were transmitted in approximately 94% of those analyzed, suggesting a false-negative rate of ~0.06.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from experimental data on transmission of homozygous variants.

claims.claim: The false-positive rate for MPAS detection of gonadal mosaic mutations in blastocysts is approximately 0.001.
claims.source: Conversely, when assessing the presence of gonadal mosaic mutations identified in one sperm donor in the blastocysts of the other two, we only found one such event out of 985 possible, suggesting an MPAS false-positive rate of ~0.001.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from experimental data on cross-contamination or false-positive detection.

claims.claim: Whole-genome-amplified blastocysts exhibit modest allelic dropout.
claims.source: Thus, this approach provides sensitivity to detect clinically relevant gonadal mosaicism (i.e., mutations with a measurable and potentially actionably abundance) and specificity to assess transmissions of perm mosaic mutations to blastocysts, and it suggests that whole-genome-amplified blastocysts exhibit modest allelic dropout, even though allelic imbalance was frequently observed.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed false-negative rate and transmission patterns.

claims.claim: The three sperm donors harbored a combined 55 detected gonadal mosaic mutations.
claims.source: The three sperm donors harbored a combined 55 detected gonadal mosaic mutations—mostly single-nucleotide mutations—with the potential to be transmitted to offspring (F01: 12, F02: 13, and F03: 30) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results, with reference to figures showing the data.

claims.claim: F01 harbored 12 gonadal mosaic mutations, F02 harbored 13, and F03 harbored 30.
claims.source: The three sperm donors harbored a combined 55 detected gonadal mosaic mutations—mostly single-nucleotide mutations—with the potential to be transmitted to offspring (F01: 12, F02: 13, and F03: 30) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This provides the breakdown of mutations per individual, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: The difference in mutation number between F01/F02 and F03 likely represents expected biological variability within the previously observed range.
claims.source: While F01 and F02 differed by more than twofold from F03, this likely represents expected biological variability that is within the previously observed range (Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed variation, supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: None of the variants were predicted to impair health when heterozygous.
claims.source: None of the variants were predicted to impair health when heterozygous, and they, thus, serve as likely neutral variants to model transmission.
claims.evidence: This describes the predicted functional impact of the identified variants.

claims.claim: The gonadal mosaic mutations were present at allelic fractions between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055).
claims.source: These mutations were present at AFs between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055), with those of lower AF typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm') and those of higher AF typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared') (Figure 1c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This provides quantitative data on the allelic fractions of detected mutations.

claims.claim: Mutations of lower allelic fraction are typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm').
claims.source: These mutations were present at AFs between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055), with those of lower AF typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm') and those of higher AF typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared') (Figure 1c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the tissue distribution pattern of mutations based on their allelic fraction.

claims.claim: Mutations of higher allelic fraction are typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared').
claims.source: These mutations were present at AFs between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055), with those of lower AF typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm') and those of higher AF typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared') (Figure 1c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the tissue distribution pattern of mutations based on their allelic fraction.

claims.claim: The number, distribution, and abundance of detected mutations were consistent with other unbiased analyses performed previously.
claims.source: Overall, their number, distribution, and abundance were consistent with other unbiased analyses performed previously (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This compares the current findings to prior published work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The sperm donor F01 (36 years of age) had an excessive number of soma-specific mutations at lower allelic fractions, evidencing early clonal hematopoiesis.
claims.source: Of note, similar to our prior observations (Yang et al., 2021), the sperm donor F01 (36 years of age) had an excessive number of soma-specific mutations ('Soma') at lower AFs, evidencing early clonal hematopoiesis (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed mutation pattern, supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: For F02, two of the eight blastocysts did not show overall high quality in the MPAS for gonadal mosaic variants and were excluded from subsequent analyses.
claims.source: For F02, two of the eight blastocysts did not show overall high quality in the MPAS for gonadal mosaic variants and thus were excluded from subsequent analyses.
claims.evidence: This describes quality control measures applied to the data.

claims.claim: Mutations of higher allelic fraction evidenced higher blastocyst transmission rates than those of lower allelic fraction.
claims.source: Consistent with a model where the risk of transmission is proportional to sperm AF, mutations of higher AF evidenced higher blastocyst transmission rates than those of lower AF (R = 0.67, p value = 2.9e−8, Pearson correlation, Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes a correlation observed in the data with statistical support.

claims.claim: The risk of transmission is proportional to sperm allelic fraction.
claims.source: Consistent with a model where the risk of transmission is proportional to sperm AF, mutations of higher AF evidenced higher blastocyst transmission rates than those of lower AF (R = 0.67, p value = 2.9e−8, Pearson correlation, Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a model supported by the observed correlation between AF and transmission rate.

claims.claim: Cosegregation of mutations of almost equal allelic fraction was observed.
claims.source: Although additional mutations may arise within earlier sperm lineages marked by prior mutations (e.g., blastocyst #2 in F03), somewhat unexpectedly, we observed cosegregation of mutations of almost equal AF (e.g., blastocyst #1 in F02 or blastocyst #6 in F03); this was reflected as a nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts in F03 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes an unexpected pattern observed in the transmission data.

claims.claim: A nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts was observed in F03.
claims.source: Although additional mutations may arise within earlier sperm lineages marked by prior mutations (e.g., blastocyst #2 in F03), somewhat unexpectedly, we observed cosegregation of mutations of almost equal AF (e.g., blastocyst #1 in F02 or blastocyst #6 in F03); this was reflected as a nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts in F03 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes a statistical pattern in the transmission data, with reference to supporting figure.

claims.claim: Some early male germ cell lineages or individual mitotic divisions are more susceptible to mutation than others.
claims.source: This suggests that some early male germ cell lineages or individual mitotic divisions are more susceptible to mutation than others, allowing stratification of sperm lineages into those with higher and those with lower mosaic load, and mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed cosegregation and nonrandom distribution patterns.

claims.claim: Mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis.
claims.source: This suggests that some early male germ cell lineages or individual mitotic divisions are more susceptible to mutation than others, allowing stratification of sperm lineages into those with higher and those with lower mosaic load, and mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of different combinations of mutations across blastocysts.

claims.claim: Different combinations of gonadal mosaic mutations were observed across blastocysts.
claims.source: Indeed, we observed different combinations of gonadal mosaic mutations across blastocysts (e.g., blastocysts #5, #6, and #9 in F03).
claims.evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the transmission data.

claims.claim: For both F01 and F02, the observed transmission rate was within the 95% confidence interval of the expectation.
claims.source: Whereas for both F01 and F02 the observed transmission rate was within the 95% confidence interval of the expectation, for F03 and across all individuals when considered in total, the transmission was slightly below what was expected (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This compares observed to expected transmission rates with statistical measures.

claims.claim: For F03 and across all individuals when considered in total, the transmission was slightly below what was expected.
claims.source: Whereas for both F01 and F02 the observed transmission rate was within the 95% confidence interval of the expectation, for F03 and across all individuals when considered in total, the transmission was slightly below what was expected (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This compares observed to expected transmission rates with statistical measures.

claims.claim: The undertransmission likely reflects a limitation of the model which assumes that gonadal mosaic mutations arise and transmit independently.
claims.source: This likely reflects a limitation of the model which assumes that gonadal mosaic mutations arise and transmit independently—a simplification, as mutations arising on the same lineage have the potential to cotransmit.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed undertransmission based on model assumptions.

claims.claim: Mutations arising on the same lineage have the potential to cotransmit.
claims.source: This likely reflects a limitation of the model which assumes that gonadal mosaic mutations arise and transmit independently—a simplification, as mutations arising on the same lineage have the potential to cotransmit.
claims.evidence: This is a biological inference about mutation transmission based on lineage relationships.

claims.claim: The undertransmission may be especially relevant if sperm lineages do not stochastically accumulate mutations during early development.
claims.source: This may be especially relevant if sperm lineages do not stochastically accumulate mutations during early development.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed undertransmission pattern.

claims.claim: The observations closely reflect expectations, suggesting that gonadal mosaicism assessment can serve as a predictor of mutation transmission.
claims.source: Nevertheless, our observations closely reflect expectations, suggesting that gonadal mosaicism assessment can serve as a predictor of mutation transmission.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of observed and expected transmission rates.

claims.claim: The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across all chromosomes except for chromosomes 19, 22, and X/Y.
claims.source: The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across all chromosomes—except for chromosomes 19, 22, and X/Y—roughly as expected based on chromosomal length.

claims.claim: The chromosomal distribution of mutations was roughly as expected based on chromosomal length.
claims.source: The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across all chromosomes—except for chromosomes 19, 22, and X/Y—roughly as expected based on chromosomal length.
claims.evidence: This compares the observed distribution to expectations based on chromosome size.

claims.claim: The vast majority of mutations was found in intergenic (n = 28) or intronic (n = 24) regions.
claims.source: As expected based on prior work, the vast majority was found in intergenic (n = 28) or intronic (n = 24) regions; one mutation each was found in a 5′-UTR, the intron of a noncoding RNA, and an exon.
claims.evidence: This describes the genomic location distribution of detected mutations.

claims.claim: One mutation was found in a 5′-UTR, one in the intron of a noncoding RNA, and one in an exon.
claims.source: As expected based on prior work, the vast majority was found in intergenic (n = 28) or intronic (n = 24) regions; one mutation each was found in a 5′-UTR, the intron of a noncoding RNA, and an exon.
claims.evidence: This describes the genomic location of specific mutations.

claims.claim: The exonic mutation (F03, AF = 0.063) resulted in a nonsynonymous SNV in RABGAP1 (NM_012197; p.Asp74Gly).
claims.source: The exonic mutation (F03, AF = 0.063) resulted in a nonsynonymous SNV in RABGAP1 (NM_012197; p.Asp74Gly), a rare, previously reported mutation (allele frequency of 7.96e−6) with no known disease association.
claims.evidence: This describes the specific characteristics of the one exonic mutation detected.

claims.claim: The RABGAP1 mutation is a rare, previously reported mutation (allele frequency of 7.96e−6) with no known disease association.

claims.evidence: This provides information about the frequency and clinical significance of the mutation.

claims.claim: Reanalysis of the REACH cohort was performed by combining the list of detected gonadal mosaic mutations with previously established variants called from trio WGS.
claims.source: Reanalysis of the REACH cohort data was performed by combining the list of detected gonadal mosaic mutation (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021) with previously established variants called from the trio WGS (Brandler et al., 2018; Brandler et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for the replication analysis using previously published data.

claims.claim: In the REACH cohort, across 131 sperm-detectable mosaic variants, nine transmissions among seven unique variants were observed.
claims.source: Across 131 sperm-detectable mosaic variants, we observed nine transmissions among seven unique variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of the replication analysis in the REACH cohort.

claims.claim: In the REACH cohort, the observed transmission rate was slightly below the expected 95% confidence interval when combining analysis of the eight families.
claims.source: As this cohort had a lower number of observable transmission events per paternal sample due to the lower number of fertilization events (1–3 offspring compared to 8–14 blastocysts) and lower sequencing depth, we combined analysis of the eight families. The observed transmission rate was again slightly below the expected 95% confidence interval (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, c).
claims.evidence: This reports the statistical comparison of observed to expected transmission in the REACH cohort.

claims.claim: The replication in live-born offspring supports the undertransmission observed in blastocysts.
claims.source: This replication in live-born offspring supports the undertransmission observed in blastocysts and highlights the potential predictive power of gonadal mosaicism assessment.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the consistency between the blastocyst and live-born offspring results.

claims.claim: The replication in live-born offspring highlights the potential predictive power of gonadal mosaicism assessment.

claims.claim: The study directly measured the abundance of gonadal mosaic variants and demonstrated transmission to preimplantation blastocysts for three couples undergoing IVF.

claims.claim: The results provide proof-of-concept that a priori detected gonadal mosaic mutations can transmit to blastocysts and therefore likely to offspring.

claims.claim: The study was only able to ascertain the phenomenon in three sperm donors and their associated blastocysts.

claims.claim: None of the variants interrogated for this study were predicted to be disease causing.

claims.claim: If this approach is to be advanced in the clinic to prevent genetic disease, further research is necessary that expands the size of the cohort and directly assesses a priori identified pathogenic variants for transmission to blastocysts.
claims.source: Thus, if this approach is to be advanced in the clinic to prevent genetic disease, further research is necessary that expands the size of the cohort and directly assesses a priori identified pathogenic variants for transmission to blastocysts.

claims.claim: Further technological development will be required to enable the direct assessment of mutations from biopsies rather than whole blastocysts.

claims.claim: Previous studies focused on the detection of mosaicism in parents following the identification of de novo mutations in offspring.

claims.claim: Following the birth of a child with a disease due to a de novo mutation, parents are provided with an empirical recurrence risk of 1–2% for future pregnancies.

claims.claim: The population recurrence risk of 1-2% reflects an average of a near-zero risk in the majority and measurably higher risk (up to 25%) in a minority of instances due to gonadal mosaicism.

claims.claim: Recent studies have improved the risk accuracy by incorporating population models and sampling parental blood.

claims.claim: Direct assessment of gonadal mosaicism can provide a more precise personalized risk and the potential to prevent recurrence through genetic testing.

claims.claim: The framework of detecting mosaicism after a child is born is only applicable to families where a de novo mutation has previously been identified.

claims.claim: This study provides the important complement that detected variants are transmitted to the next generation.

claims.claim: 1 in 15 males carry a potentially pathogenic mutation, detectable in approximately 5% of sperm cells.

claims.claim: Gonadal mosaic variants likely represent approximately 15% of the monogenic sporadic component of diseases such as autism or congenital heart disease.
claims.source: While this likely only represents ~15% of the monogenic sporadic component of diseases such as autism or congenital heart disease, this is the sole fraction that could be prevented with further advances.
claims.evidence: This is an estimate of the proportion of disease attributable to gonadal mosaicism.

claims.claim: Gonadal mosaic variants represent the sole fraction of monogenic sporadic disease that could be prevented with further advances.
claims.source: While this likely only represents ~15% of the monogenic sporadic component of diseases such as autism or congenital heart disease, this is the sole fraction that could be prevented with further advances.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the preventability of different types of de novo mutations.

claims.claim: If mosaic mutations were detected prior to pregnancy and mutation-carrying blastocysts were identified by PGT, there could be positive consequences for families through the prevention of pregnancy termination or pediatric diseases.
claims.source: Thus, if these mosaic mutations were detected prior to pregnancy, and if mutation-carrying blastocysts were identified by PGT, there could be positive consequences for families through the prevention of pregnancy termination or pediatric diseases.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical benefits of the approach.

results.result: The study recruited three couples undergoing IVF and used deep whole-genome sequencing (~300× depth) with the MSMF computational pipeline to identify male gonadal mosaicism, followed by targeted ultra-deep genotyping (MPAS) to validate variants and assess transmission to 32 preimplantation blastocysts.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C27-C32 collectively describe the study design, recruitment, and methodology. The approach is well-documented with appropriate sequencing depth, validated computational pipelines (C32 cites >95% sensitivity and 90% specificity), and clear sample sizes. The methodology is internally consistent and builds on prior validated work.

results.result: The three sperm donors harbored 55 gonadal mosaic mutations (F01: 12, F02: 13, F03: 30) at allelic fractions between 0.003-0.247 (mean: 0.047), with lower AF mutations typically sperm-specific and higher AF mutations shared between sperm and somatic tissues, consistent with prior unbiased analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C44 describe the detection and characterization of gonadal mosaic mutations. The data are presented with quantitative measures (C40), tissue distribution patterns (C41-C42), and comparison to prior work (C43). The observation of clonal hematopoiesis in F01 (C44) is supported by citations and figure references. The results are internally consistent.

results.result: Across 55 gonadal mosaic variants, 15 were transmitted to blastocysts for 19 total transmission events, with transmission rates positively correlated with sperm allelic fraction (R=0.67, p=2.9e-8), demonstrating that gonadal mosaic mutations detected in sperm can transmit to preimplantation blastocysts.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C25, C45-C47 present the core transmission findings with statistical support. The correlation between AF and transmission (C46-C47) is statistically significant with appropriate testing. Quality control measures were applied (C45). The result directly addresses the study's main hypothesis with quantitative evidence.

results.result: The MPAS genotyping approach on whole-genome-amplified blastocyst material demonstrated a false-negative rate of ~0.06 and false-positive rate of ~0.001, indicating modest allelic dropout but high specificity for detecting gonadal mosaic mutation transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 describe the technical validation of the detection method. The false-negative rate was calculated from homozygous variant transmission (expected 100%, observed 94%), and false-positive rate from cross-sample contamination testing (1/985 events). These are appropriate validation approaches with clear quantitative results.

results.result: Cosegregation of mutations with similar allelic fractions and nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts (particularly in F03) suggests that some early male germ cell lineages are more susceptible to mutation than others, and that mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 describe patterns in mutation transmission with statistical support (C49 references Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing permutation analysis). The inference about differential lineage susceptibility (C50-C51) is reasonable given the observed cosegregation patterns, though it remains somewhat speculative about mechanism.

results.result: Observed transmission rates were within the 95% confidence interval of expectations for F01 and F02, but slightly below expectations for F03 and across all individuals combined, likely reflecting model limitations assuming independent mutation transmission when mutations on the same lineage can cotransmit.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 compare observed to expected transmission with appropriate statistical measures (95% CI). The interpretation of undertransmission (C55-C57) acknowledges model limitations regarding independence assumptions. The conclusion that observations closely reflect expectations (C58) is reasonable given the modest deviation and is supported by Figure 3.

results.result: Reanalysis of the REACH cohort (8 families, 14 offspring, 131 sperm-detectable variants) showed 9 transmissions among 7 unique variants, with observed transmission slightly below the expected 95% confidence interval, replicating the undertransmission pattern observed in blastocysts and supporting the predictive power of gonadal mosaicism assessment.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 and C9 describe the replication analysis using previously published data. The methodology is clearly described (C65), results are quantified (C66-C67), and the consistency with blastocyst findings strengthens the main conclusions (C68-C69). The replication in live-born offspring provides important validation despite lower statistical power due to fewer offspring per family.

results.result: The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across chromosomes roughly as expected by length (excluding chr 19, 22, X/Y), predominantly in intergenic (n=28) or intronic (n=24) regions, with one exonic nonsynonymous mutation in RABGAP1 (p.Asp74Gly) that is rare and has no known disease association.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 describe the genomic distribution and functional annotation of detected mutations. The chromosomal distribution (C59-C60) and regional distribution (C61-C62) are consistent with expectations. The characterization of the single exonic mutation (C63-C64) is appropriately detailed. These are descriptive findings that support the neutrality of variants used for modeling.

results.result: The study provides proof-of-concept that a priori detected gonadal mosaic mutations can transmit to preimplantation blastocysts and likely to offspring, with assessment at the blastocyst stage avoiding potential selection bias during implantation or survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 and C26 summarize the main conclusion. The proof-of-concept is supported by the transmission data (19 events across 15 variants). The rationale for studying blastocysts (C26) is methodologically sound to avoid selection bias, though the extrapolation to offspring (C71) is reasonable but not directly demonstrated in this cohort.

results.result: The study has important limitations: only three sperm donors were assessed, and none of the interrogated variants were predicted to be disease-causing, requiring future research with larger cohorts and pathogenic variants, as well as technological development for biopsy-based assessment.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 appropriately acknowledge study limitations. The small sample size (C72) and lack of pathogenic variants (C73) are significant constraints on clinical applicability. The recommendations for future work (C74-C75) are reasonable and necessary before clinical implementation. This honest assessment of limitations is appropriate.

results.result: Unbiased preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism may represent a feasible approach to reduce transmission of potentially harmful de novo mutations, potentially reducing their impact on miscarriages and pediatric disease through embryo selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C24, C80, and C89 make speculative statements about clinical applications. While the proof-of-concept is demonstrated, the study only examined neutral variants (C73), and clinical feasibility requires validation with pathogenic variants, larger cohorts, and biopsy-based methods (C74-C75). The potential benefits are plausible but not yet demonstrated.

results.result: Background context establishes that de novo mutations underlie pediatric congenital disorders, mosaic mutations can be detected in parental tissues (particularly sperm at 5-20% of pathogenic mutations), every male harbors dozens of gonadal mosaic mutations independent of age, but experimental evidence of transmission of prospectively identified gonadal mosaic mutations was lacking.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C23 provide background context supported by multiple citations to prior work. These establish the scientific rationale and identify the knowledge gap (C23) that the study addresses. The claims about prevalence (C17-C19), age-independence (C20-C21), and clinical significance (C16, C22) are appropriately cited to prior literature.

results.result: Previous approaches focused on detecting mosaicism after identifying de novo mutations in offspring, providing empirical recurrence risks of 1-2% that mask heterogeneity (near-zero to 25% risk), whereas this study demonstrates prospective detection and transmission assessment, complementing prior work on detection capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 contextualize the study's contribution relative to prior work. The description of current clinical practice (C77-C78) and limitations of reactive approaches (C81-C82) are appropriately cited. The claim that this study provides an important complement (C84) is supported by the transmission data demonstrating prospective prediction capability.

results.result: Based on prior estimates, 1 in 15 males carry potentially pathogenic mutations detectable in ~5% of sperm, potentially affecting 1 in 300 concepti, representing ~15% of monogenic sporadic disease that could theoretically be prevented.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 present estimates about population-level impact. While C85 is cited to prior work, the prediction about 1 in 300 concepti (C86) and the 15% estimate (C87) involve extrapolations with uncertainty. The claim that this is the 'sole fraction' preventable (C88) is speculative and may not account for future advances in preventing other de novo mutation types.
